hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: Replacing ApoE4-associated CE(20:4) with CE(18:1) significantly reduced neuronal acidic-compartment tau-fibril accumulation.
rows.Finding quote: Indeed, CE(18:1)-lipApoE4 produced significantly lower accumulation of pHrodo-tau pffs than CE(20:4)-lipApoE4 (Figure 6L–M), consistent with lipofuscin-potentiated tau pff accumulation.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE4 cargo CE(20:4) -> CE(18:1)) -> (less endolysosomal tau-fibril accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Human NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons; 14-day 20 μg/mL lipidated ApoE4 pretreatment followed by 14 days of 2.5 μg/mL pHrodo-P301S-tau fibrils; ApoE replenished during incubation; confocal imaging.

rows.Finding description: Human neurons treated with PUFA-cholesteryl-ester–ApoE4 accumulated more lipofuscin than ApoE3-treated neurons after 21 days.
rows.Finding quote: Therefore, we assessed the pathogenic potential of peroxidation-prone PUFA-CE by treating iNeurons with CE(20:4)-lipApoE isoforms. We observed accumulation of lipofuscin along with an established toxic product of arachidonic acid peroxidation, 4-HNE, following the allelic series of ApoE4 > ApoE3 > ApoE2.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4 carrying CE(20:4)) -> (more neuronal lysosomal lipofuscin)
rows.Experimental system: Human doxycycline-inducible NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons, Sigma 66540561; CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE initially 20 μg/mL, replenished weekly with 10 μg/mL; 21-day exposure; autofluorescence imaging.

rows.Finding description: Replacing peroxidation-prone CE(20:4) with CE(18:1) in ApoE4 particles abolished lipofuscin induction in human H4 cells.
rows.Finding quote: Replacing CE(20:4) with CE(18:1) in the POPC-ApoE4 lipoproteins abolished lipofuscin induction (Figure 5J–K), denoting a PUFA requirement.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE4 cargo CE(20:4) -> CE(18:1)) -> (loss of lipofuscin induction)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells; three-day 20 μg/mL CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE4 versus CE(18:1)/POPC-ApoE4 exposure; lipofuscin autofluorescence.

rows.Finding description: After fourteen days, neuronal lipofuscin increasingly distinguished CE(20:4)-ApoE4 from ApoE3, with greater accumulation after ApoE4 treatment in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: After longer incubation (14 d and 21 d), a progressively larger difference between ApoE4 and ApoE3 emerged (Figure S5G, Figure 5B).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4 carrying CE(20:4)) -> (more fourteen-day neuronal lipofuscin)
rows.Experimental system: Human NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons; 14-day CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE treatment, initially 20 μg/mL and replenished after seven days; autofluorescence imaging.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S5E and S5G, quantification

rows.Finding description: In three independent H4-cell experiments, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 and CE(20:4)-ApoE4 modestly but significantly reduced lysosomal cathepsin activity relative to low-lipofuscin treatments; an E4–E3 difference was not reported.
rows.Finding quote: Cathepsin activity measured by the 6QC probe40 showed a modest but significant reduction with CE(20:4)-lipApoE3 or CE(20:4)-lipApoE4 treatment compared to other treatments that minimally induced lipofuscin (Figure S6G–H).
rows.Finding summary: (CE(20:4)-ApoE4 versus low-lipofuscin treatments) -> (lower lysosomal cathepsin activity)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells; three-day CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE isoform or CE(18:1)/POPC-ApoE treatment; 5 μM fluorogenic 6QC probe for two hours; live imaging of cathepsin-dependent fluorescence.

rows.Finding description: Replacing ApoE4-associated CE(20:4) with CE(18:1) prevented the neuronal lipofuscin phenotype in the tau-fibril accumulation experiment.
rows.Finding quote: To confirm the effect of PUFA-CE-lipApoE4 on tau pff accumulation is causally linked to lipofuscin, we directly compared CE(20:4)-lipApoE4 with CE(18:1)-lipApoE4, which did not induce lipofuscin as CE(18:1) is not prone to peroxidation (Figure 6J–K).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE4 cargo CE(20:4) -> CE(18:1)) -> (less neuronal lipofuscin)
rows.Experimental system: Human NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons; 14-day 20 μg/mL CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE4 or CE(18:1)/POPC-ApoE4 pretreatment followed by 14 days with 2.5 μg/mL pHrodo-tau fibrils and continued ApoE replenishment; autofluorescence.

rows.Finding description: Blocking receptor engagement with LDLR extracellular domain dramatically reduced ApoE4–PUFA-cholesteryl-ester–induced lipofuscin in human neurons.
rows.Finding quote: LDLR ECD co-treatment with CE(20:4)-lipApoE4 dramatically reduced lipofuscin (Figure 5F–G), confirming LDLR dependency.
rows.Finding summary: (CE(20:4)-ApoE4 + LDLR competition) -> (less neuronal lipofuscin)
rows.Experimental system: Human NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons, Sigma 66540561; three-day treatment with 20 μg/mL CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE4, with or without 20 μg/mL LDLR ECD; autofluorescence imaging.

rows.Finding description: Human neurons pretreated with CE(20:4)-ApoE4 accumulated more acidic-compartment tau-fibril signal than ApoE3-treated neurons, especially among lipofuscin-positive cells, across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: After another 13–14 d incubation, total pHrodo signals from tau pffs that were internalized and accumulated in the endolysosomes demonstrated a trend of ApoE4 > ApoE3 > ApoE2 > K146E ApoE4, with the isoform-dependent difference being more pronounced among lipofuscin-positive neurons (Figure 6H–I), suggesting neuronal accumulation of tau pffs is augmented by a higher lipofuscin load.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4 carrying CE(20:4)) -> (more endolysosomal tau-fibril accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Human NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons, Sigma 66540561; 14-day CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE pretreatment, initially 20 μg/mL; 2.5 μg/mL pHrodo-labeled P301S tau fibrils for another 13 days; all neurons and cells with more than three lipofuscin spots analyzed.

rows.Finding description: CE(20:4)-ApoE3 and CE(20:4)-ApoE4 caused prominent LAMP1-positive lysosomal clustering in three independent H4-cell experiments; the text did not establish a difference between those isoforms.
rows.Finding quote: LAMP1 immunostaining revealed no treatment effect on the total lysosomal area, but CE(20:4)-lipApoE3/E4 treatment resulted in prominent lysosomal clustering (Figure S6I–K), a phenotype previously observed in association with lysosomal impairment41,42.
rows.Finding summary: (CE(20:4)-ApoE3 or ApoE4 treatment) -> (greater LAMP1-positive lysosomal clustering)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells after three-day lipidated ApoE treatment; fixed-cell LAMP1 immunostaining; clustering index calculated from clustered versus total LAMP1 spot area.

rows.Finding description: Introducing the Christchurch receptor-binding mutation into ApoE4 significantly attenuated PUFA-cholesteryl-ester–induced lipofuscin in human H4 cells.
rows.Finding quote: Lastly, CE(20:4)-lipidated Christchurch mutants showed significantly attenuated lipofuscinosis (Figure 7F–G).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE4 -> ApoE4 R136S carrying CE(20:4)) -> (less lipofuscin)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells; three-day 20 μg/mL CE(20:4)/POPC-lipidated ApoE isoforms and Christchurch variants; lipofuscin autofluorescence imaging.

rows.Finding description: In human astrocytes, ApoE4 produced greater internalized ApoE signals and occupancy of LAMP1 compartments than ApoE3; printed ApoE-positive LAMP1 fractions were 0.497 ± 0.090 versus 0.410 ± 0.049.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE isoform differences were manifested in the differential levels of internalized lipApoE (ApoE4 > ApoE3 > ApoE2), giving rise to the same isoform trend for LAMP1-positive vesicles containing ApoE immunoreactivity (Mander’s coefficients = 0.266 ± 0.045 for ApoE2, 0.410 ± 0.049 for ApoE3, 0.497 ± 0.090 for ApoE4) (Figure 2I).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (greater ApoE accumulation and ApoE occupancy of LAMP1 compartments)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE-KO iPSC-derived astrocytes originating from ThermoFisher A18945, originally APOE3/3; 10 μg/mL POPC-ApoE for one day; super-resolution immunofluorescence and Mander’s overlap analysis.

rows.Finding description: Human H4 cells reproduced isoform-dependent lipofuscin accumulation after PUFA-cholesteryl-ester–ApoE treatment, with LDLR extracellular domain blocking the phenotype.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE isoform-dependent lipofuscin accumulation was replicated in WT H4 and HAP1 cells, similarly blocked by LDLR ECD or KO of LDLR, but not LRP1 (Figure 5H–I, Figure S5H–I).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4 carrying CE(20:4)) -> (greater lipofuscin burden)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells, ATCC HTB-148; three-day 20 μg/mL CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE treatment, with or without 20 μg/mL LDLR ECD; autofluorescence imaging.

rows.Finding description: After seven days, ApoE3- and ApoE4-associated CE(20:4) produced weak neuronal lipofuscin whereas ApoE2 produced minimal signal, in three independent experiments; an E4–E3 difference was not stated.
rows.Finding quote: At 7 d, lipofuscin induced by CE(20:4)-lipApoE3/E4 was weakly detectable, while signals for CE(20:4)-ApoE2 were minimal.
rows.Finding summary: (CE(20:4)-ApoE3 or ApoE4 treatment) -> (early neuronal lipofuscin accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Human NGN2 iPSC-derived neurons, Sigma 66540561; seven-day 20 μg/mL CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE exposure; live lipofuscin autofluorescence, normalized using endpoint nuclear counts.

rows.Finding description: Lipidated ApoE treatments produced no reported treatment effect on total LAMP1-positive lysosomal area in three independent H4-cell experiments.
rows.Finding quote: LAMP1 immunostaining revealed no treatment effect on the total lysosomal area, but CE(20:4)-lipApoE3/E4 treatment resulted in prominent lysosomal clustering (Figure S6I–K), a phenotype previously observed in association with lysosomal impairment41,42.
rows.Finding summary: (Lipidated ApoE treatment, including ApoE3 and ApoE4) -> (no change in total lysosomal area)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells after three-day CE(20:4)/POPC-ApoE isoform or CE(18:1)/POPC-ApoE treatment; total LAMP1 spot area quantified by immunofluorescence.

rows.Finding description: Internalized ApoE3 and ApoE4 localized predominantly to LAMP1 compartments, with printed Mander’s coefficients of 0.903 ± 0.024 and 0.900 ± 0.008, respectively; no significance comparison was reported.
rows.Finding quote: Super-resolution imaging on APOE KO iAstrocytes confirmed internalized lipApoE completely colocalized with endogenous LDLR (Mander’s coefficient for ApoE puncta with colocalizing LDLR = 1 for all 3 isoforms), largely inside LAMP1 compartments (Figure 2H) (Mander’s coefficients for ApoE puncta with colocalizing LAMP1 = 0.823 ± 0.061 for ApoE2; 0.903 ± 0.024 for ApoE3; 0.900 ± 0.008 for ApoE4).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (similar proportion of internalized ApoE localized to LAMP1 compartments)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE-KO A18945-derived iPSC astrocytes; one-day 10 μg/mL POPC-ApoE treatment; super-resolution ApoE, LDLR and LAMP1 imaging.

rows.Finding description: ApoE3 and ApoE4 similarly promoted acidic-compartment HDL accumulation relative to ApoE2 or no ApoE, and LDLR extracellular domain suppressed both; an ApoE4-specific functional defect was not established.
rows.Finding quote: Pre-complexing pHrodo-HDL with ApoE isoforms promoted its uptake in the order of ApoE4 ~ ApoE3 > ApoE2 (Figure 3A, C). LDLR ECD suppressed pHrodo-HDL uptake with ApoE3 or ApoE4, indicating a key role of LDLR in ApoE-mediated HDL internalization.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (similar acidic-compartment HDL accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Human H4 neuroglioma cells; one-day treatment with 10 μg/mL pHrodo-HDL precomplexed with 10 μg/mL recombinant ApoE, with or without 20 μg/mL LDLR ECD; confocal imaging.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: Donor 1 APOE4/4 astrocytes had lower lysosomal DQ-BSA proteolysis than isogenic APOE3/3 astrocytes; the legend reports three to four biological replicates without assigning donor-specific counts.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4/4 astrocytes showed significantly reduced lysosomal DQ-BSA signal compared to isogenic control APOE3/3 astrocytes across two isogenic donor pairs (Donor #1: p= 0.0032; Donor #2: p < 0.0001, Figure 4d), indicating decreased lysosomal proteolytic activity.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower lysosomal proteolytic activity in Donor 1 astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived astrocytes, CRISPR-isogenic APOE3/3 and APOE4/4; DQ-BSA cleavage assessed after 24 hours by flow cytometry in DAPI-negative cells.

rows.Finding description: APOE4/4 astrocytes retained significantly lower DQ-BSA proteolytic activity than APOE3/3 astrocytes after normalization to co-internalized, proteolysis-resistant dextran.
rows.Finding quote: To distinguish between reduced lysosomal number and reduced lysosomal function per organelle, we normalized DQ-BSA fluorescence to co-internalized dextran, which accumulates in the lysosomes but is resistant to proteolysis76. Even after dextran normalization, APOE4/4 astrocytes retained significantly lower proteolytic activity (p = 0.0098; Figure S4e), indicating functional impairment rather than solely reduced lysosome abundance.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower dextran-normalized lysosomal proteolytic activity in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived astrocytes, isogenic APOE3/3 and APOE4/4; DQ-BSA cleavage normalized to co-internalized proteolysis-resistant dextran; supplementary assay timing and sample size unavailable.

rows.Finding description: In APOE4/4 astrocytes, 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin significantly increased lysosomal DQ-BSA proteolysis compared with vehicle, with four biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: Treatment with 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (2HβCD) and methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) significantly increased lysosomal proteolysis (2HβCD: p = 0.0002; MβCD: p = 0.019) (Figure 5b), whereas the other interventions had neutral or negative effects on APOE4/4 lysosomal proteolytic activity (Figure 5b).
rows.Finding summary: (2HβCD-mediated cholesterol reduction in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher lysosomal proteolytic activity)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived APOE4/4 astrocytes; 100 μM 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin versus vehicle; drug protocol includes four days of pretreatment followed by reseeding and maturation under treatment; DQ-BSA Red integrated fluorescence over 24 hours and area under the curve.

rows.Finding description: Methyl-β-cyclodextrin significantly increased lysosomal proteolytic activity in APOE4/4 astrocytes from the second donor.
rows.Finding quote: Increased lysosomal proteolytic activity with MβCD was replicated in astrocytes from a second donor (p = 0.0045; Figure S5c).
rows.Finding summary: (MβCD-mediated cholesterol reduction in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher lysosomal proteolytic activity in Donor 2)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 2 KOLF2.1J iPSC-derived APOE4/4 astrocytes, Clone A JIPSC001150; methyl-β-cyclodextrin treatment, specified as 100 μM in methods; replication of the DQ-BSA lysosomal proteolysis rescue; supplementary timing and sample-size details unavailable.

rows.Finding description: After extracellular α-Syn removal, APOE4/4 astrocytes showed no significant decrease in intracellular α-Syn fluorescence over 24 hours, whereas APOE3/3 astrocytes cleared it, with four biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: To assess degradation, extracellular α-Syn was removed after 24 hours, and intracellular α-Syn-HiLyte signal was tracked for an additional 24 hours. APOE3/3 astrocytes showed a significant reduction in intracellular α-Syn-HiLyte signal (p < 0.0001), whereas APOE4/4 astrocytes showed no significant decrease (p = 0.694; Figure 4c), indicating impaired degradation of α-Syn.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (impaired intracellular clearance of exogenous α-Syn in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Human AG09173 iPSC-derived astrocytes, CRISPR-isogenic APOE3/3 and APOE4/4; 2 μg/mL α-Syn-HiLyte exposure for 24 hours followed by washout and another 24 hours; intracellular fluorescence measured by confocal imaging as the degradation/clearance readout.

rows.Finding description: APOE4/4 astrocytes showed significantly less colocalization of internalized α-Syn with LysoTracker-positive lysosomes than APOE3/3 astrocytes after four hours.
rows.Finding quote: To validate that the α-Syn was being endocytosed into the endolysosomal pathway, we incubated astrocytes with α-Syn-HiLyte for 4 hours and co-stained with LysoTracker. In agreement with our other findings that APOE4/4 astrocytes have impaired α-Syn uptake, the percentage of α-Syn-HiLyte that co-localized with LysoTracker decreased in APOE4/4 astrocytes compared to APOE3/3 (p = 0.0395; Figure S5f).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower lysosomal localization of exogenous α-Syn in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived astrocytes, isogenic APOE3/3 and APOE4/4; four-hour α-Syn-HiLyte incubation followed by LysoTracker costaining; percentage of α-Syn signal colocalizing with acidic lysosomal compartments.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig 5F, vehicle-treated APOE4/4 versus APOE3/3

rows.Finding description: Methyl-β-cyclodextrin significantly increased α-Syn colocalization with LysoTracker-positive lysosomes in APOE4/4 astrocytes compared with vehicle.
rows.Finding quote: However, APOE4/4 astrocytes treated with MβCD showed increased colocalization of α-Syn-HiLyte with LysoTracker compared to vehicle-treated APOE4/4 astrocytes (p = 0.0343).
rows.Finding summary: (MβCD-mediated cholesterol reduction in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher lysosomal localization of exogenous α-Syn)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived APOE4/4 astrocytes; methyl-β-cyclodextrin versus vehicle, with 100 μM specified in the drug-treatment methods; four-hour α-Syn-HiLyte incubation and LysoTracker colocalization assay.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig 5F, MβCD versus vehicle in APOE4/4 astrocytes

rows.Finding description: Methyl-β-cyclodextrin-treated APOE4/4 astrocytes showed no significant difference in α-Syn lysosomal localization from vehicle-treated APOE3/3 astrocytes, a null genotype contrast after rescue.
rows.Finding quote: Strikingly APOE4/4 astrocytes treated with MβCD showed similar α-Syn lysosomal localization as vehicle-treated APOE3/3 astrocytes (p = 0.946; Figure S5f).
rows.Finding summary: MβCD-treated APOE4/4 and vehicle-treated APOE3/3 astrocytes showed no statistically significant difference in α-Syn lysosomal localization.
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived astrocytes, isogenic APOE3/3 and APOE4/4; vehicle-treated APOE3/3 compared with methyl-β-cyclodextrin-treated APOE4/4, with 100 μM specified in methods; four-hour α-Syn-HiLyte and LysoTracker colocalization assay.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig 5F, MβCD-treated APOE4/4 versus vehicle-treated APOE3/3

rows.Finding description: Donor 1 APOE4/4 astrocytes had significantly lower LAMP1 immunoreactivity than isogenic APOE3/3 astrocytes, indicating reduced lysosomal compartment signal.
rows.Finding quote: Consistent with this, immunoreactivity for the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 was also significantly reduced in APOE4/4 astrocytes compared to isogenic APOE3/3 astrocytes (Donor #1: p = 0.0002 and Donor #2: p = 0.0001, Figure S4d).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower LAMP1-positive lysosomal compartment signal in Donor 1 astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived astrocytes, CRISPR-isogenic APOE3/3 and APOE4/4; LAMP1 immunostaining; assay-specific timing and supplementary quantification details unavailable.

rows.Finding description: Methyl-β-cyclodextrin significantly increased LysoTracker-positive lysosomal signal in APOE4/4 astrocytes; the legend reports five to six biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: Consistent with improved lysosomal capacity, MβCD increased LysoTracker-positive lysosomal signal in APOE4/4 astrocytes (p = 0.044; Figure 5d), with similar effects observed across donors (2HβCD: p < 0.0001; MβCD: p < 0.0001, Figure S5d).
rows.Finding summary: (MβCD-mediated cholesterol reduction in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher LysoTracker-positive lysosomal signal)
rows.Experimental system: Human Donor 1 AG09173 iPSC-derived APOE4/4 astrocytes; 100 μM methyl-β-cyclodextrin versus vehicle following the astrocyte drug-treatment protocol; LysoTracker fluorescence normalized to Hoechst area; dye signal is a surrogate influenced by lysosomal abundance and acidity.
rows.Data location: Fig 5D, MβCD versus vehicle in APOE4/4 astrocytes

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: Across two experiments, Aβ1–42-induced lysosomal leakage occurred in more than 25% of apoE4-transfected cells versus 15% of apoE3-transfected cells.
rows.Finding quote: Lysosomal leakage was seen in only 15% of the neo- and apoE3-transfected cells but in more than 25% of the apoE4-transfected cells (Fig. 2A).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater proportion of cells with Aβ1–42-induced lysosomal leakage)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells stably expressing human apoE3 or apoE4; Lucifer Yellow loading followed by aggregated Aβ1–42 at 20 μM for 20 h at 37 °C, as specified by reference to Fig 1; fluorescence microscopy scoring diffuse cytosolic staining across 15 fields, approximately 30 cells per field; two experiments.

rows.Finding description: Aβ1–42 increased cytosolic β-hexosaminidase activity by approximately 85% in apoE4 cells and approximately 30% in apoE3 cells across two experiments performed in duplicate.
rows.Finding quote: A treatment increased cytosolic -hexosaminidase activity to a significantly greater extent in apoE4-transfected cells than in neo- and apoE3-transfected cells (85% versus 40 and 30%, respec- tively; p  0.001).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater Aβ1–42-induced release of lysosomal β-hexosaminidase into cytosol)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells stably expressing human apoE3 or apoE4; grown to approximately 90% confluence and treated with aggregated Aβ1–42 at 20 μM for 24 h at 37 °C; cytosolic fractions isolated by homogenization and ultracentrifugation; β-hexosaminidase activity assayed in 20 μg cytosolic protein; two experiments in duplicate. This measures enzyme leakage, not loss of intrinsic catalytic activity.

rows.Finding description: After aggregated Aβ1–42 treatment, more apoE4- than apoE3-transfected Neuro-2a cells showed diffuse Lucifer Yellow fluorescence, indicating greater lysosomal leakage.
rows.Finding quote: After treatment with A1–42, however, it was readily apparent that more apoE4-transfected Neuro-2a cells than neo- or apoE3-transfected cells displayed a diffuse intracellular pattern of fluorescence, indicating lysosomal leak- age into the cytosol (Fig. 1, arrows).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater Aβ1–42-induced lysosomal membrane leakage)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells stably expressing human apoE3 or apoE4, generally secreting 80 ng apoE/ml medium/24 h; Lucifer Yellow loading at 100 μg/ml for 20 h, washing, then aggregated Aβ1–42 at 20 μM for 20 h at 37 °C; confocal microscopy. Aβ was aggregated for 72 h at 37 °C before use.

rows.Finding description: In two experiments, apoE4 also increased Aβ1–40-induced lysosomal leakage relative to apoE3, although less markedly than with Aβ1–42.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE4 also potentiated lysosomal leakage induced by A1–40 (Fig. 2A), albeit to a lesser extent than that induced by A1–42.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater Aβ1–40-induced lysosomal leakage)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells stably expressing human apoE3 or apoE4; Lucifer Yellow loading followed by aggregated Aβ1–40 at 20 μM for 20 h at 37 °C, following the Fig 1 protocol; diffuse cytosolic fluorescence scored in 15 fields, approximately 30 cells per field; two experiments.

rows.Finding description: Without Aβ treatment, neither apoE3- nor apoE4-transfected Neuro-2a cells showed significant lysosomal leakage; no significant difference between isoforms was reported.
rows.Finding quote: No significant ly- sosomal leakage was observed in untreated apoE3- or apoE4- transfected cells.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in detectable baseline lysosomal leakage)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells stably transfected with human apoE3 or apoE4 genomic DNA, generally secreting 80 ng apoE/ml medium/24 h; untreated controls after Lucifer Yellow loading at 100 μg/ml for 20 h at 37 °C; confocal microscopy of punctate versus diffuse fluorescence. No donor age or human brain cells were studied.
rows.Data location: Fig 1, untreated top row; Results, ApoE4 Potentiates Aβ-induced Lysosomal Leakage

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: In mouse N2a cells, inhibitor-derived lysosomal Aβ42 degradation was greater with apoE3 than apoE4, with apoE3 producing 1.75-fold the degradation measured with apoE4.
rows.Finding quote: When lysosomal degradation of Aβ42 was calculated by subtracting the cell-associated Aβ in the absence of inhibitors from that in the presence of inhibitors, apoE3 enhanced Aβ42 lysosomal degradation by 1.75-fold when compared with apoE4 ( Fig. 5 B ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower inhibitor-derived lysosomal Aβ42 degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a neuroblastoma cells; recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4, 500 nM, with Aβ42, 500 nM, for 24 h in serum-free medium, with or without pepstatin A, leupeptin, and E-64d; degradation calculated as cell-associated Aβ42 with inhibitors minus that without inhibitors, using ELISA. Lipid metabolism was not measured.

rows.Finding description: Inhibitor-derived lysosomal degradation of apoE4 was lower than that of apoE3 in mouse N2a cells exposed to Aβ42.
rows.Finding quote: We found that apoE3 was transported into lysosomes and degraded more efficiently than apoE4 ( Fig. 7 , A and B ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower inhibitor-derived lysosomal apoE degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a neuroblastoma cells; recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4, 500 nM, with Aβ42, 500 nM, for 24 h, with or without lysosomal inhibitors; degraded apoE calculated as cell-associated apoE with inhibitors minus that without inhibitors, using ELISA. Lipid metabolism was not measured.

rows.Finding description: Confocal imaging of mouse N2a cells treated with lysosomal inhibitors showed less lysosome-associated Aβ42 with apoE4 than apoE3, with the image comparison quantified in Fig 5D.
rows.Finding quote: In addition, confocal microscopy also revealed that internalized FAM-Aβ42, which was largely co-localized with LysoTracker, was greatly increased in the presence of apoE ( Fig. 5 C ). Upon quantification, we confirmed that the amounts of Aβ42 in lysosomes were higher in apoE3-treated cells than apoE4-treated cells ( Fig. 5 D ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower Aβ42 delivery to LysoTracker-positive compartments)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a neuroblastoma cells; FAM-Aβ42, 500 nM, and recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4, 500 nM, for 24 h with lysosomal inhibitors; LysoTracker Red, 75 nM, during the final hour; confocal fluorescence microscopy. This was a localization assay, not a calibrated lysosomal pH assay; lipid metabolism was not measured.
rows.Data location: Fig 5C, representative images quantified in Fig 5D

rows.Finding description: Quantification of confocal images showed less Aβ42 associated with lysosomes in apoE4-treated mouse N2a cells than in apoE3-treated cells during lysosomal inhibition.
rows.Finding quote: Upon quantification, we confirmed that the amounts of Aβ42 in lysosomes were higher in apoE3-treated cells than apoE4-treated cells ( Fig. 5 D ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower lysosome-associated Aβ42)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a neuroblastoma cells; FAM-Aβ42, 500 nM, with recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4, 500 nM, for 24 h with lysosomal inhibitors; LysoTracker Red, 75 nM, during the final hour; ImageJ quantification of lysosome-associated Aβ fluorescence. Lipid metabolism was not measured.

rows.Finding description: Immunostaining of mouse N2a cells during lysosomal inhibition showed less efficient trafficking of apoE4 than apoE3 to LAMP1-positive lysosomal compartments.
rows.Finding quote: The more efficient trafficking of apoE3 than apoE4 was confirmed by immunostaining and confocal microscopy ( Fig. 7 , C and D ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (less efficient apoE trafficking to LAMP1-positive compartments)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a neuroblastoma cells; recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4, 500 nM, with Aβ42, 500 nM, for 24 h in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors; immunostaining for apoE and LAMP1 followed by confocal microscopy. Lipid metabolism was not measured.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: In SH-SY5Y cells, 27-OHC produced stronger lysosomal δ-secretase activation with rApoE4 than with rApoE3. The authors also report leakage into the cytoplasm with rApoE4. Figure 1H–I represents three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Remarkably, 27-OHC strongly augmented δ-secretase levels and triggered its activation in the lysosomes in the presence of rApoE4, and the stimulatory effects were much stronger than with rApoE3. Notably, rApoE4 potently stimulated δ-secretase FL leakage from the lysosomes into the cytoplasm with most of active and truncated δ-secretase under rApoE4 and 27-OHC treatment.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4, with 27-OHC) -> (stronger lysosomal δ-secretase activation and aberrant δ-secretase trafficking)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells treated with 100 nM rApoE3 or rApoE4 and 10 μM 27-OHC for three days. Lysosomal and cytosolic fractions were immunoblotted. The Results identify the secretion sample as rat neuronal medium, while the joint legend groups medium collection with SH-SY5Y fractionation.
rows.Data location: Fig 1H-I, cited jointly; individual H/I allocation is not specified in supplied text.

rows.Finding description: In the SH-SY5Y fractionation experiment, cholesterol failed to elicit cytosolic translocation of active δ-secretase. The authors also report no active-enzyme secretion under cholesterol, but the Results and legend give conflicting accounts of the medium source.
rows.Finding quote: By contrast, cholesterol weakly activated δ-secretase in the lysosomes in the presence of rApoE4 but not rApoE3, but it failed to elicit active δ-secretase cytosolic translocation or secretion (Figure 1H-I).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 and apoE4 cholesterol conditions) -> (no detected cytosolic translocation of active δ-secretase)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y cells treated with 100 nM rApoE3 or rApoE4 and 50 μM cholesterol for three days, followed by subcellular fractionation and immunoblotting. The Results call the medium rat neuronal medium. The joint figure legend groups it with SH-SY5Y samples.
rows.Data location: Fig 1H-I, cited jointly; individual H/I allocation is unspecified.

rows.Finding description: In the SH-SY5Y experiment reported jointly in Fig 1H-I, cholesterol weakly activated lysosomal δ-secretase with apoE4 but not apoE3 across three independent experiments, indicating increased enzyme activation rather than demonstrated degradation failure.
rows.Finding quote: By contrast, cholesterol weakly activated δ-secretase in the lysosomes in the presence of rApoE4 but not rApoE3, but it failed to elicit active δ-secretase cytosolic translocation or secretion (Figure 1H-I).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4, with cholesterol) -> (weak lysosomal δ-secretase activation)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells; recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4, 100 nM, and cholesterol, 50 μM, for three days; lysosomal/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting.
rows.Data location: Fig 1H-I, cited jointly; individual H/I allocation is unspecified.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: APOE4-expressing astrocytes showed defective autophagic cargo degradation relative to APOE3-expressing astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: In these astrocytes, autophagy was found to be defective at the initiation step (autophagosome formation) and at the cargo degradation step.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (impaired autophagic cargo degradation in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: APOE3- and APOE4-expressing astrocytes, reported from Simonovitch et al. (2016). Species, cell source, age, cargo, assay and conditions for this particular comparison are not specified.

rows.Finding description: APOE4 astrocytes showed reduced lysosomal degradation of mitochondria-associated LC3-II and p62 relative to APOE3 astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: In addition, the interaction of the autophagic proteins LC3-II and p62 with the mitochondria, and the lysosomal degradation of mitochondrial LC3-II and p62 were reduced in APOE4 astrocytes.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (reduced lysosomal degradation of mitochondrial LC3-II and p62 in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: APOE3- and APOE4-expressing astrocytes in the discussion of Schmukler et al. (2020). Species, cell source, age, lysosomal-degradation assay, treatments and observation interval are unspecified.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: Human isogenic iPSC-derived APOE4/4 oligodendroglia showed significantly more Bodipy-cholesterol colocalization with Lysotracker-Red than APOE3/3 oligodendroglia, with four biological replicates and four images averaged per replicate.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 oligodendroglia exhibited significantly (p = 0.0069) more Bodipy-cholesterol co-localized with Lysotracker-Red staining than APOE3/3, suggesting lysosomal accumulation of cholesterol in APOE4 oligodendroglia (Extended Data Fig. 7d).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased lysosomal cholesterol accumulation in human iPSC-derived oligodendroglia)
rows.Experimental system: Human iPSC-derived oligodendroglia from an isogenic APOE3/3–APOE4/4 experimental framework using reciprocal editing of a cognitively normal APOE3/3 donor line and an APOE4/4 AD donor line; the specific donor pair used for this panel is not identified in the supplied text. Cells were differentiated and matured in vitro; no aged-cell model was specified. Bodipy-cholesterol colocalization with Lysotracker-Red was quantified using ImageJ with identical thresholds across conditions.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: Across three biological replicates, mouse astrocytes expressing human APOE4 had lysosomal pH elevated by >1 pH unit compared with APOE3 astrocytes, indicating impaired lysosomal acidification without testing lipid metabolism.
rows.Finding quote: In contrast, we observed >1 pH unit elevation of lysosomal pH in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig. 3 C ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher lysosomal pH in mouse astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic knock-in of human ApoE3 or ApoE4, supplied by David M. Holtzman; donor age and mouse background not specified. Lysosomal pH measured by ratiometric flow cytometry after 12 h loading with pHrodo-green–dextran and Alexa Fluor 647–dextran followed by a 6 h chase; ionophore-based calibration. These are mouse cells, not human brain cells; lipid metabolism was not measured.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: After two weeks of thiorphan treatment, APOE4 mouse CA1 neurons showed larger and more abundant cathepsin D-positive lysosomes and more diffuse granular cathepsin D staining than APOE3 neurons, supporting altered lysosomal morphology without establishing impaired function.
rows.Finding quote: Double-labeling confocal microscopy, using the lysosomal marker cathepsin D, revealed that the CA1 neurons of the thiorphan-treated apoE4 mice contained intracellular punctate cathepsin D-positive lysosomes, the size and levels of which were markedly higher than those of the corresponding apoE3 mice, as well as increased levels of diffused granular cathepsin D staining ( Fig. 8 ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (larger and more abundant cathepsin D-positive lysosomes and increased diffuse cathepsin D staining)
rows.Experimental system: Male human APOE3/3 versus APOE4/4 targeted-replacement mice, backcrossed eight generations to C57BL/6J, aged 3–4 months at experimentation; intracerebroventricular infusion of 0.5 mM thiorphan at 0.25 μl/h for two weeks; hippocampal CA1 neurons examined by cathepsin D/Aβ double-labeling confocal microscopy; no lipid manipulation, lysosomal enzyme activity assay, pH measurement, or degradation assay reported for this comparison.
rows.Data location: Fig 8, cathepsin D images and associated lysosomal-activation Results paragraph
